value: The process of overseeing and planning new product development, advertising, promotions and sales.
reason: The old back rests on the lead sentence marked “citation needed”; the article gives a second, untagged definition, used here.

value: Marketing management is defined as the process of overseeing and planning new product development, advertising, promotions and sales.
reason: Evidence to match the new back.

value: To plan that work it uses tools from economics and competitive strategy, such as analysis of strategic groups of competitors and value chain analysis, to study the firm’s industry.
reason: Keeps the cited tools sentence and says why they matter.

value: Criteria for goals and objectives, named by the mnemonic acronym SMART, in which each letter stands for one criterion.
reason: The front asks for the criteria but the back called them an acronym; the primer teaches two terms (SMART criteria, SMART) and should separate them.

value: Knowing the letters means knowing the criteria: in George T. Doran’s original form they are specific, measurable, assignable, realistic and time-related (the article’s opening says time-bound).
reason: The old explanation called ‘time-bound’ the original form; the History section gives Doran’s original T as ‘Time-related’. The article contradicts itself (lead vs History); the deck’s fact cards teach the History half.

value: A matrix, also called the BCG matrix, that helps corporations analyse their business units, that is, their product lines.
reason: The primer introduces two registry terms; the back should say they name the same thing.

value: The micro is customers, partners and competitors; the macro is the larger society’s forces, which act on the micro.
reason: The article contradicts itself: it says the micro-environment consists of customers, partners and competitors (cited), then adds ‘the public’ as a final aspect in an uncited paragraph ending in “citation needed”. The primer teaches three; this card taught four.

value: A country’s birth rate has fallen for a decade, so fewer children will need school shoes. For a children’s shoe maker, which level of the environment does this change belong to?
reason: A new law is disputable: the article also puts a ‘government public’ that passes laws in the micro-environment. A demographic trend is macro without dispute.

value: Demography is one of the forces of the larger society that the source places in the macroenvironment, and those forces act on the microenvironment.

A: the microenvironment is customers, partners and competitors, not a society-wide trend. C: the internal environment lies inside the firm. D: the meso level concerns the design of infrastructure and sector policy.
reason: Matches the new scenario; drops ‘publics’, which rests on uncited text.

value: The macro-environment refers to all forces that are part of the larger society and that affect the micro-environment. It encompasses factors such as demography, the economy, natural forces, technology, politics, and culture, among others.
Economists have proposed several definitions since the 1950s with no clear consensus; this one stresses a cost that only the newcomer has to bear.
reason: The article says there is no consensus definition; the card presented one as the definition, while later cards use Porter’s wider list of barriers.

value: For example, consumer law and antitrust law (discrimination and health-and-safety law are others).
reason: The article lists labour law under political factors and employment law under legal ones; naming employment law invites confusion.

value: External ones come from outside the person, such as culture, social class, family and the buying situation; internal ones are personal and interpersonal factors.
reason: The article defines internal influences as ‘personal and interpersonal factors’, not ‘within the person’, and lists culture and reference groups under both headings.

value: The line is not sharp: the source lists culture, sub-culture and reference groups as external influences, but also counts them as social-identity factors among internal ones.
reason: States the article’s self-contradiction; the card teaches the external-influences section.

value: The source lists reference groups among external influences (it also names them as social-identity factors), and a group she admires and hopes to join is aspirational.
reason: Hedges the article’s overlap; the answer stays the only defensible option.

value: A: physiological needs are bodily basics such as air, water, food and sleep. C: esteem needs concern respect from others and self-respect. D: self-actualisation is realising one’s full potential.
reason: The article lists shelter under both physiological and safety needs; dropping it avoids teaching one half of that contradiction in a distractor.

value.alt: A five-band pyramid. From the base up: physiological, safety, love and belonging, esteem, self-actualisation. A note says the most fundamental needs sit at the base and that Maslow did not draw the pyramid himself.
